selectedCourseEvidence.description2: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
selectedCourseEvidence.name: Personal & Professional Development
selectedCourseEvidence.profile: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.
selectedCourseEvidence.topics: Scholarly sources and research questions; Argumentation and thesis statements; Literature synthesis; Academic integrity and referencing; Community engagement; Personal learning goals and reflective learning; Collaborative learning; Self-efficacy; Stress and time management; Responsible use of AI
selectedCourseEvidence.methods: Scholarly literature searching and source evaluation; Literature synthesis; CARS model for research introductions; Reflective development planning; Community project co-design

selectedCourseEvidence.description2: This course includes a multi-faceted exploration of AI’s business, managerial, economic and related societal implications. Designed for students with a strong interest in AI, it requires no prior technical background.
selectedCourseEvidence.name: Business & Economy in the Age of AI
selectedCourseEvidence.profile: Examines AI's business, economic and societal implications without requiring a technical background. AI foundations and limitations lead into applications across enterprise functions and industries, labour-market change, productivity, innovation, market structure and inequality. Governance, corporate responsibility, regulation and future scenarios connect technological developments to institutional choices. Students analyze business cases and competing scholarly arguments, then investigate a country's AI readiness, workforce, regulation and industrial policy.
selectedCourseEvidence.topics: AI capabilities and limitations; AI in business functions and industries; Agentic AI; Market structure and business models; Automation and augmentation; Labour markets and productivity; Innovation and economic growth; Inequality; Techno-economic paradigms and economic narratives; AI ethics and societal impacts; Corporate governance and AI regulation; National AI readiness and industrial policy; Future AI scenarios
selectedCourseEvidence.methods: Business-case analysis; Comparative analysis of economic arguments; Evidence-based policy argumentation; Comparative country AI-readiness analysis

selectedCourseEvidence.description2: Explore how individuals, firms, and societies make economic decisions. This course introduces key concepts from both microeconomics and macroeconomics, including markets, incentives, and the principles of supply and demand, and provides a foundation for analyzing real-world economic issues.
selectedCourseEvidence.name: Introduction to Economics
selectedCourseEvidence.profile: Introduces microeconomic principles and short-run macroeconomic analysis. The microeconomic component examines supply and demand, strategic interaction, consumer choice, production, costs and competitive markets. The macroeconomic component introduces output, unemployment and inflation, then relates goods and financial markets through the IS-LM model. Students use algebra and graphs to explain economic behaviour and apply models to economic issues.
selectedCourseEvidence.topics: Supply and demand; Game theory; Rational consumer choice; Individual and market demand; Production and costs; Perfect competition; Aggregate output; Unemployment and inflation; Goods and financial markets; IS-LM model
selectedCourseEvidence.methods: Algebraic and graphical economic analysis; Supply-and-demand analysis; Game-theoretic analysis; IS-LM modelling

selectedCourseEvidence.description2: Investigate the role of government in the economy, focusing on how public policy influences efficiency and equity. The course covers taxation, public goods, externalities, and government spending. Combining theoretical models with empirical evidence, it evaluates how different policies affect societal welfare.
selectedCourseEvidence.name: Public Economics
selectedCourseEvidence.profile: Examines government intervention through the efficiency and equity effects of public policy. Market failure, public goods and externalities provide foundations for studying public production, collective choice, spending and taxation. Health, education, welfare and social insurance illustrate expenditure and redistribution questions. Students apply economic models, interpret data and graphs, evaluate research and develop a research proposal and paper.
selectedCourseEvidence.topics: Role and size of government; Market efficiency and failure; Public goods; Externalities; Efficiency and equity; Public production; Public choice; Public expenditure; Health and education policy; Welfare programs; Social insurance; Taxation and redistribution
selectedCourseEvidence.methods: Economic model-based policy analysis; Efficiency and equity assessment; Interpretation of economic data and graphs; Critical evaluation of public-economics research

selectedCourseEvidence.description2: The course explores how companies develop strategies and drive responsible digital transformation amid rapid technology change impacting the economy and society. Students develop a strategic plan, from vision to execution, and identify digital value opportunities. Using industry cases, they gain foresight into digital technologies and their impact on strategy, business models and social responsibilities.
selectedCourseEvidence.name: Strategy & Digital Transformation

selectedCourseEvidence.description2: This course examines the institutional, political and cultural forces shaping global businesses. It first explores how international companies operate, then centers on key global challenges including cross-border governance, corporate responsibility, geopolitical strategies and global trade. It provides a comprehensive understanding of today’s complex international business environment.
selectedCourseEvidence.name: International Business & Governance
selectedCourseEvidence.profile: Examines how international trade, globalization and political, sociocultural and technological forces shape firms' cross-border decisions. Economic foundations include trade theories, foreign direct investment, foreign exchange and the monetary system. Students analyze governance, responsibility and trade-policy conflicts, investigate an international-business question, and develop an evidence-based market-entry strategy covering country attractiveness and business functions. A tariff case applies game theory to stakeholder choices and negotiation.
selectedCourseEvidence.discipline: International business; International economics; Strategic management
selectedCourseEvidence.topics: Globalization; International trade theories; Foreign direct investment; Foreign exchange and international monetary systems; Trade policy and economic integration; Cross-border governance; Corporate responsibility; Sociocultural and technological business environments; International business strategy; Market entry; Marketing, supply chains and human resources; Economic warfare
selectedCourseEvidence.methods: Trade-policy case analysis; Game-theoretic stakeholder analysis; Secondary-data analysis and visualization; Country and market-attractiveness assessment; Market-entry strategy development; Research-question formulation and evidence evaluation

selectedCourseEvidence.description2: Through experiential learning, students turn their own bold ideas into new ventures. No prior business expertise is required as teams work on a startup project from ideation to final pitch while gaining business and entrepreneurial skills in areas such as design thinking, business model and customer validation. The class fosters creativity and collaboration to drive business and social innovation.
selectedCourseEvidence.name: Entrepreneurship & Business Foundations
selectedCourseEvidence.profile: Introduces entrepreneurship and core business functions through the development of a startup concept. Students use design thinking to discover customer needs, define a problem, generate and prototype solutions, and construct value propositions and business models. Marketing, finance, operations, human resources and funding inform a coherent business plan and investor pitch. Entrepreneurial cases and a startup simulation examine decision-making, early growth and business lifecycles, with attention to societal impact and sustainability.
selectedCourseEvidence.topics: Entrepreneurial mindset and pathways; Business environments, ownership and competition; Customer needs; Value propositions; Business models; Marketing and sales; Finance and accounting; Venture funding; Operations and human resources; Competitive positioning; Startup growth and business lifecycles; Sustainability and societal impact
selectedCourseEvidence.methods: Design thinking; Customer-needs discovery; Ideation and prototyping; Value Proposition Canvas; Business Model Canvas; Business planning; SWOT and risk assessment; Startup simulation

selectedCourseEvidence.description2: Research Methods & Statistics gives you a strong foundation in how business management—and social and behavioral sciences—move from mere practices to true fields of scientific study. You’ll learn how to plan research logically, from designing studies to working with real data using experimental and survey techniques. You’ll also study descriptive and inferential statistics, with a brief intro to multivariate tools.
selectedCourseEvidence.name: Research Methods & Statistics
selectedCourseEvidence.profile: Introduces empirical research design and statistical analysis, followed by a substantial student research project. Students study operationalization, measurement quality, sampling, surveys and experimental and nonexperimental designs, then descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression. R and R Commander support data display and analysis. Project teams develop instruments and a research plan, collect and analyze data, and report results under explicit research-ethics and privacy requirements.
selectedCourseEvidence.topics: Scientific inquiry and hypotheses; Operationalization and measurement; Reliability and validity; Survey construction and sampling; Randomized and quasi-experimental designs; Nonexperimental and qualitative research; Descriptive statistics; Sampling distributions and estimation; Hypothesis testing and confidence intervals; Association and regression; Research ethics and anonymous data collection
selectedCourseEvidence.methods: Survey design; Probability and nonprobability sampling; Experimental and nonexperimental research design; R and R Commander data analysis; Descriptive statistics and visualization; Scale-reliability analysis; One- and two-sample mean tests; ANOVA; Chi-square tests; Correlation and regression; Empirical data collection and analysis

selectedCourseEvidence.description2: Personal Leadership provides a comprehensive introduction to leadership theory and practice, designed to help students discover their unique leadership style through self-awareness and practical skill-building. Through interactive workshops, reflective exercises, and real-world applications, students engage deeply with core leadership principles and develop the tools needed to lead confidently in any setting.
selectedCourseEvidence.name: Personal Leadership
selectedCourseEvidence.profile: Introduces leadership through self-leadership, leadership theory and emotional intelligence. Covey's habits provide a framework for personal vision, prioritization and collaboration, alongside transformational, authentic, situational and adaptive leadership perspectives. Students analyze personality and emotional-intelligence profiles in relation to group dynamics, examine leadership cases, and construct a personal development plan with actionable goals. Assessment tools support educational reflection rather than diagnosis, and the outline acknowledges differences in their scientific support.
selectedCourseEvidence.topics: Self-leadership and self-awareness; Covey's seven habits; Emotional intelligence and emotion regulation; Personality and group dynamics; Transformational and authentic leadership; Situational and adaptive leadership; Evolutionary perspectives on leadership; Goal setting and prioritization; Conflict resolution and negotiation; Trust and collaboration
selectedCourseEvidence.methods: Leadership theory and case analysis; Reflective personality and emotional-intelligence assessments; Eisenhower prioritization matrix; SMART goal setting; Leadership-development planning; Leadership simulations

selectedCourseEvidence.description2: This course blends theory with practice from both fiction and the real world, helping you develop essential leadership skills. Learn how to inspire teams, sharpen your communication, take ethical decisions, and lead with confidence.
selectedCourseEvidence.name: Leadership Communication
selectedCourseEvidence.profile: Studies leadership communication through leadership theory, persuasion and practical rhetorical work. Students compare contemporary leadership approaches and examine emotional intelligence, gender, culture and ethics. Literary characters, film and speeches provide material for analyzing effective and ineffective leadership. Students interview a real leader, analyze the leader's communication challenge in an advisory report, and develop a public address presenting their own ethical leadership vision.
selectedCourseEvidence.topics: Leadership models and approaches; Transformational, authentic and adaptive leadership; Servant leadership and followership; Emotional intelligence; Leadership ethics; Gender and culture in leadership; Persuasion and organizational communication; Leadership in literature and film; Storytelling and public speaking; Personal leadership vision
selectedCourseEvidence.methods: Leadership-theory application; Literary and film-based leadership analysis; Professional interviewing and note collection; Leadership-discourse analysis; Communication-advisory report development; Rhetorical speechwriting and storytelling

selectedCourseEvidence.description2: What does it take to lead effectively through pressure, conflict, and diversity? Explore how emotion, identity, belonging, and inclusion shape leadership, teamwork, and performance. Design and conduct an original empirical study while building career-ready skills in research design, data analysis, teamwork, ethical decision-making, and scientific communication.
selectedCourseEvidence.name: Psychology of Leading Under Pressure
selectedCourseEvidence.profile: Examines how emotion regulation, emotional intelligence, emotional expression and suppression, emotional labor, belonging, identity safety and psychological safety shape leadership and social interaction under conflict, exclusion and interpersonal uncertainty. It emphasises inclusive leadership and ethnic, cultural, sexual and gender minority experiences, with digital emotion regulation as a further strand. Students conduct a supervised quantitative survey project: formulating theory-driven hypotheses, selecting established psychological measures, designing and piloting a Qualtrics survey, recruiting participants ethically, collecting original data and preparing a clean dataset. Individual work applies descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, correlations, group comparisons and introductory multiple regression in SPSS or RStudio, and interprets findings and limitations in empirical reports and evidence-based leadership recommendations.
selectedCourseEvidence.discipline: Leadership studies; Social psychology; Work and organizational psychology; Psychological measurement; Quantitative social research
selectedCourseEvidence.topics: Emotion regulation strategies; Emotional intelligence; Emotional expression and suppression; Emotional labor; Inclusive leadership; Belonging and identity safety; Psychological safety; Ethnic, cultural, sexual and gender minority experiences; Digital emotion regulation; Psychological measurement, reliability and validity; Ethical survey research in diverse populations; Interpretation and limitations of quantitative evidence; Evidence-based leadership recommendations
selectedCourseEvidence.methods: Theory-driven hypothesis formulation; Quantitative survey research; Established psychological measure selection and evaluation; Qualtrics survey construction and piloting; Ethical participant recruitment and original data collection; Codebook development, reverse coding and scale scoring; Data cleaning and missing-data documentation; Descriptive statistics; Reliability analysis; Correlation analysis; Group comparisons; Introductory multiple regression in SPSS or RStudio; APA-style empirical reporting

selectedCourseEvidence.description2: This course offers Liberal Arts and Sciences students a deep dive into the psychological, social, and structural dynamics that shape workplaces. Through interactive case discussions, simulations, and real-world insights, students develop critical skills in motivation, leadership, group dynamics, and culture. By synthesizing research and applying theory to practice, participants gain the tools to navigate and influence diverse organizational environments effectively.
selectedCourseEvidence.name: Psychology of Organizations & Leadership
selectedCourseEvidence.profile: Examines organizational behaviour at individual, group and organizational levels. Topics connect personality, perception, emotions and motivation to teams, leadership, power, conflict, structure, culture and change. Students design research plans for organizational cases and conduct a brief systematic literature review using PRISMA reporting tools. Workshops develop literature searching, study selection, source appraisal and synthesis, linking organizational-psychology evidence to practical questions and recommendations.
selectedCourseEvidence.topics: Diversity, equity and inclusion; Job attitudes and satisfaction; Emotions, stress and workplace health; Personality and individual differences; Perception and decision-making; Motivation; Group behaviour and work teams; Human resource systems; Communication, conflict and negotiation; Leadership, power and politics; Organizational structure; Organizational culture and change
selectedCourseEvidence.methods: Organizational case analysis; Research design and hypothesis formulation; Systematic literature review; PRISMA flow diagrams and checklists; Database searching and study screening; Source-quality appraisal and evidence synthesis

selectedCourseEvidence.description2: How do you get to yes? In this course you will learn how to craft persuasive arguments, deploy the right language, negotiate more effectively, and influence decisions with confidence—whether in business, leadership, or life.
selectedCourseEvidence.name: Negotiation & Strategic Thinking
selectedCourseEvidence.profile: Develops negotiation as an analytical practice and interpersonal skill. Students learn interest-based bargaining, BATNA and ZOPA, value creation, framing, concessions and strategies for handling power, emotions and difficult counterparts. Social-psychological and communication perspectives connect negotiation to trust, ethics, culture and relationships. Frequent simulations and narrative analysis lead to an annotated negotiation film and the design, teaching and evaluation of a negotiation scenario grounded in Delta Climate Center themes.
selectedCourseEvidence.discipline: Negotiation studies; Strategic management; Social psychology; Communication studies
selectedCourseEvidence.topics: Interests versus positions; BATNA and ZOPA; Mutual gains and objective criteria; Dual-concern model; Anchoring, framing and concessions; Trade-offs and logrolling; Cognitive biases and influence; Power and emotions; Trust, reputation and ethics; Cross-cultural and organizational negotiation; Negotiation implementation and withdrawal; Stakeholder interests
selectedCourseEvidence.methods: BATNA and ZOPA analysis; Stakeholder-interest mapping; Interest-based negotiation; Negotiation simulations; Narrative and film analysis of bargaining; Negotiation-scene scripting and annotation; Scenario design and reflective evaluation

selectedCourseEvidence.description2: Introduces the sustainable engineering approach of working with natural processes for flood protection, land reclamation and port development. Covers history and principles of ecosystem‑based design, explores case studies and includes guest lectures and field excursions.
selectedCourseEvidence.name: Building with Nature
selectedCourseEvidence.profile: Introduces approaches that combine human infrastructure with natural processes and ecosystem health, with particular attention to Zeeland and the history of water management on Walcheren. Students examine applications across sandy and muddy coasts, lowland lakes, rivers and estuaries, cities and ports. Projects investigate ecological connectivity and formulate a Building with Nature intervention; a practical wall-building project explores constructed structures.
selectedCourseEvidence.topics: Nature-based infrastructure; Coastal and water management; Walcheren's water-management history; Sandy and muddy coasts; Lowland lakes; Rivers and estuaries; Urban nature-based solutions; Harbour habitats; Habitat connectivity; Ecoducts and fish ladders
selectedCourseEvidence.methods: Building with Nature case analysis; Ecological-corridor project analysis; Nature-based intervention design; Construction and testing of model walls

selectedCourseEvidence.description2: Explores sustainable water management in delta regions. Focuses on adaptation to rising seas, floods and land subsidence; engages students in projects in Zeeland; and highlights nature‑based solutions and resilient infrastructure.
selectedCourseEvidence.name: Living with Water
selectedCourseEvidence.profile: Examines how delta societies manage water risks and opportunities, using Zeeland as a central case. Physical and ecological challenges such as flooding, salinization, freshwater scarcity, subsidence and pollution are connected to infrastructure, history, governance, law and justice. Students evaluate engineered and nature-based responses, considering trade-offs and long-term consequences. Site-based inquiry and a project apply these concepts to context-sensitive adaptation in a delta region.
selectedCourseEvidence.discipline: Water management; Environmental governance; Delta sustainability
selectedCourseEvidence.topics: Delta environments; Flood risk and protection; Drainage and freshwater management; Sea-level rise and subsidence; Salinization; Water infrastructure and ecological consequences; Water governance, law and justice; Contaminants and pollution; EU Water Framework Directive; Nature-based adaptation; Urban ecology and water; Long-term delta resilience
selectedCourseEvidence.methods: Site-based water-management case analysis; Comparative appraisal of engineered and nature-based solutions; Context-sensitive adaptation-strategy development

selectedCourseEvidence.description2: Examines strategies and technologies towards a circular economy. Explores resource security and stewardship, develops lab skills and inorganic chemistry knowledge, and connects to themes at the Delta Climate Center.
selectedCourseEvidence.name: R3: Recycling, Recovery, Remediation
selectedCourseEvidence.profile: Studies resource circularity through solar-panel recycling, metal recovery from electronic waste, and soil remediation using plants and mycelium. Theory and extensive laboratory work connect material composition and separation technologies to resource yields, environmental consequences and recycling constraints. Students develop leaching protocols, analyze metal concentrations and recovery, cultivate fungal networks, and use microscopy to characterize materials and mycelium growth.
selectedCourseEvidence.discipline: Environmental chemistry; Materials recycling; Environmental biotechnology
selectedCourseEvidence.topics: Circular resource supply; Solar-cell and solar-panel recycling; Delamination and material separation; Electronic waste; Pyrometallurgy and hydrometallurgy; Precious-metal recovery; Plastic-recycling legislation; Phytoremediation; Mycoremediation; Mycelium-based soil amendments
selectedCourseEvidence.methods: Solar-panel dismantling and physical separation; Chemical leaching; Experimental-protocol design; ICP metal analysis; Electrochemical recovery; Scanning electron microscopy and EDS; Mycelium cultivation and growth characterization; Recovery-yield and resource-potential calculations

selectedCourseEvidence.description2: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.
selectedCourseEvidence.name: Governance of Sustainability
selectedCourseEvidence.profile: Analyzes sustainability as a problem of collective decision-making involving governments, markets and civil society. Concepts of institutions, power, participation, justice and problem complexity frame competing technological and systemic responses. Structured cases examine food, freshwater, energy and climate mitigation. Students apply governance frameworks to a Zeeland issue, consult relevant organizations or experts, and produce policy advice or an evaluation assessing effectiveness, feasibility and stakeholder interests.
selectedCourseEvidence.discipline: Environmental governance; Public policy; Political science
selectedCourseEvidence.topics: Institutions, actors and power; Collective action and common-pool resources; Governance modes and networks; Techno-optimism and ecological limits; Climate justice; Populism and environmental politics; Wicked and long-term problems; Public participation; Food, water and energy governance; Markets, public goods and externalities; Adaptive and global governance; Climate mitigation; Policy effectiveness and feasibility
selectedCourseEvidence.methods: Governance-framework application; Problem diagnosis and causal analysis; Stakeholder and policy-option matrices; Policy evaluation; Policy-advice memo development; Stakeholder and expert interviewing; Comparative analysis of normative policy perspectives

selectedCourseEvidence.description2: This course explores environmental conservation through biological and social science perspectives. Topics include biodiversity importance, threats to ecosystems, conservation methods, and tools to monitor and protect nature. It also covers national and international laws, policies, and initiatives aimed at preserving ecosystems and ensuring a sustainable future for current and future generations.
selectedCourseEvidence.name: Conservation Biology
selectedCourseEvidence.profile: Introduces conservation biology through biodiversity loss, its human causes and possible responses. Students examine habitat destruction and fragmentation, overharvesting, invasive species, climate change, disasters and extinction, followed by conservation planning, species management and conservation in altered landscapes. A local threatened-species project investigates conservation status and protection measures and develops a public-awareness flyer.
selectedCourseEvidence.topics: Biodiversity and ecosystems; Anthropogenic extinction; Habitat loss and fragmentation; Overharvesting; Invasive species; Climate impacts; Natural and human-caused disasters; Conservation priorities; Endangered-species management; Human-modified landscapes; People and conservation; Conservation-study design and evaluation
selectedCourseEvidence.methods: Threatened-species conservation-status analysis; Assessment of species-protection measures; Evidence-based conservation communication

selectedCourseEvidence.description2: Provides key concepts in physics, chemistry, materials science, mathematics and modelling necessary for sustainability. Uses a case study to connect concepts to real‑world sustainability challenges and prepares students for 200‑level sustainability courses.
selectedCourseEvidence.name: Sustainability Essentials I
selectedCourseEvidence.profile: Uses planetary boundaries to introduce scientific tools for understanding sustainability and human impacts on Earth systems. Students interpret graphs and uncertainty, build simple dynamic models, and learn chemical, thermodynamic and mechanical principles relevant to environmental processes. Topics connect climate, ocean acidification, nutrient cycles, energy and materials. An iterative laboratory project makes starch-based biopolymers and measures their strength and elasticity to improve the formulation.
selectedCourseEvidence.discipline: Sustainability science; Applied mathematics; Chemistry; Physics
selectedCourseEvidence.topics: Planetary boundaries and the Anthropocene; Exponential growth and environmental change; Graphs, rates and uncertainty; Dynamic systems; Chemical bonds, reactions and equilibria; Ocean acidification and nutrient cycles; Thermodynamics and entropy; Greenhouse gases and energy; Ozone depletion; Newtonian mechanics, stress and strain; Biopolymers and material properties
selectedCourseEvidence.methods: Graph interpretation and comparison; Fermi estimation; Difference-equation and first-order linear differential-equation modelling; Elementary differentiation and integration; Biopolymer preparation; Strength and elasticity measurement; Iterative experimental improvement

selectedCourseEvidence.description2: Builds on Sustainability Essentials I. Applies tools and knowledge to a real‑world sustainability case study and allows students to delve deeper into aspects connected to their field of interest.
selectedCourseEvidence.name: Sustainability Essentials II
selectedCourseEvidence.profile: Connects wave physics, chemistry and materials science to sustainability questions. Students study wave behaviour and observation methods, chemical analysis, microscopic material structure and macroscopic stress and strain. Practical sessions include wave applications and chemistry laboratory work. Reflective inquiries and a final project critically assess sustainability campaigns, identify greenwashing and communicate evidence-based improvements to a public audience.
selectedCourseEvidence.discipline: Physics; Chemistry; Materials science; Sustainability studies
selectedCourseEvidence.topics: Electromagnetic and mechanical waves; Wave composition and interference; Optical spectroscopy; Electron microscopy; Inorganic and organic chemistry; Chemical testing; Material structure and crystallography; Stress and strain; Sustainable material design; Geological wave applications; Nuclear power and waste; Greenwashing
selectedCourseEvidence.methods: Oscilloscope wave visualization; Optical-spectroscopy interpretation; Fourier wave analysis; Copper dissolution and chemical analysis; Laboratory logbook documentation; Stress-strain analysis; Mohr's-circle application; Evidence-based greenwashing case analysis; Public sustainability-communication design

selectedCourseEvidence.description2: Focuses on drivers and impacts of anthropogenic climate change on sea level, ocean acidification, ecology and society. Discusses adaptation and mitigation solutions, including renewable energy systems, carbon storage and climate‑adaptive planning, and examines climate governance and justice.
selectedCourseEvidence.name: Climate Change
selectedCourseEvidence.profile: Introduces climate-change science, societal impacts, and mitigation and adaptation. Students examine greenhouse gases, feedbacks, tipping points, ocean acidification and sea-level rise, then consequences for ecosystems, agriculture, transport, buildings and health. Climate justice, governance, communication and misinformation connect physical changes to social responses. Solution pathways include energy systems, carbon removal and climate-adaptive planning. Students interview a stakeholder and produce a short film, alongside reflection on their own role.
selectedCourseEvidence.discipline: Climate science; Environmental studies; Climate governance
selectedCourseEvidence.topics: Anthropogenic climate change; Greenhouse gases; Feedback loops and tipping points; Ocean acidification and sea-level rise; Biosphere impacts; Agriculture, transport and construction; Climate and health; Climate justice and governance; Paris Agreement; Renewable energy and sustainable heat; Carbon removal and geoengineering; Climate communication and misinformation; Climate anxiety; Mitigation and adaptation
selectedCourseEvidence.methods: Stakeholder interviewing; Short-film production for climate communication; Source-credibility evaluation; What? So What? Now What? reflective model

selectedCourseEvidence.description2: Teaches evaluation of environmental impacts of products, processes and services throughout their lifecycle. Emphasises strategic planning for a circular economy through hands‑on learning.
selectedCourseEvidence.name: Life Cycle Analysis & Circular Economy
selectedCourseEvidence.profile: Develops life-cycle approaches to evaluating products, processes and services within a circular economy. Students examine environmental, social and health consequences from resource extraction to disposal or reuse, together with costs, revenues and management strategies. Three preliminary projects develop different parts or forms of life-cycle analysis, followed by a project that integrates the stages into a full product or process assessment.
selectedCourseEvidence.discipline: Sustainability science; Industrial ecology; Life-cycle engineering and management
selectedCourseEvidence.topics: Circular economy; Product and process life cycles; Resource extraction and reuse; Environmental impacts; Social and health consequences; Life-cycle management strategies; Product-based and process-based assessment; Costs and revenues; Sustainable product and process planning
selectedCourseEvidence.methods: Life-cycle assessment; Life-cycle management strategy analysis; Environmental-impact estimation; Cost and revenue analysis; Integrated product or process assessment

selectedCourseEvidence.description2: Develops skills to recognise and handle misinformation. Discusses cognitive biases and detection methods, distinguishes real from fake experts, and includes case studies and a video project tackling a misinformation topic.
selectedCourseEvidence.name: Calling Bullshit
selectedCourseEvidence.profile: Examines misinformation through philosophy, history, psychology and practical information evaluation. Students distinguish misleading discourse from related concepts, investigate cognitive and social vulnerabilities, and analyze pseudoscience, statistical misrepresentation and reasoning errors. Fact-checking, deepfake production and response exercises develop recognition and intervention skills. Projects map a misinformation narrative's actors and circulation and produce a research-grounded myth-debunking video with an external interview.
selectedCourseEvidence.discipline: Misinformation studies; Psychology; Applied epistemology; Science communication
selectedCourseEvidence.topics: Bullshit, lying and misinformation; Historical hoaxes and propaganda; Cognitive bias and motivated reasoning; Social identity and information overload; Scientific credibility and pseudoscience; Publication bias and misconduct; Misleading statistics and data displays; Reasoning fallacies; Deepfakes; Misinformation diffusion; Debunking and counter-narratives; Medical and climate misinformation
selectedCourseEvidence.methods: Source-credibility evaluation; Fact-checking protocols; Reasoning-fallacy detection; Critical analysis of statistical claims; Misinformation-network mapping; Deepfake video construction and analysis; Debunking-message design; Expert interviewing; Documentary-style explanatory video production

selectedCourseEvidence.description2: Teaches assessment of energy usage patterns and strategies for reducing consumption or transitioning to cleaner energy. Explores solar, wind and bioenergy solutions and includes technical and economic analysis; students deliver a report and presentation to a partner company.
selectedCourseEvidence.name: Renewable System Design

selectedCourseEvidence.description2: Examines law from legal, socio‑scientific and normative perspectives. Explores definitions, legal traditions and fields of law, investigates the relationship between law and society and the concept of justice, and includes case law, excursion to international legal organisations, interviews with practitioners and a moot court session.
selectedCourseEvidence.name: Law, Society & Justice
selectedCourseEvidence.profile: Introduces law through legal, social and normative perspectives. Students compare major legal traditions and survey public and private law, including constitutional, criminal, international, human-rights, property, contract and tort law. The second part examines justice, social control and change, race and gender. Case briefs, legal interpretation, demand letters and mock trials apply legal reasoning; a family-law topic supports the design of a small socio-legal research proposal.
selectedCourseEvidence.topics: Legal positivism and empirical and normative perspectives; Common-law and civil-law traditions; Constitutional and administrative law; Criminal law; International law and human rights; Property, contract and tort law; Justice; Law and social control; Law and social change; Race and gender in law; Family law
selectedCourseEvidence.methods: Legal interpretation; Case-law research and IRAC case briefing; Demand-letter drafting; Mock-trial legal argumentation; Socio-legal research design; Literature review

selectedCourseEvidence.description2: Offers a legal, historical and philosophical approach to human rights. Studies classical and modern philosophers, traces the rise of human rights, examines the US Bill of Rights and the French Declaration, and discusses human rights treaties.
selectedCourseEvidence.name: Human Rights: Law & Philosophy
selectedCourseEvidence.profile: Studies human rights both as positive law and as philosophical claims. Students examine the UDHR, European and UN protection systems, monitoring institutions and landmark cases alongside natural law, natural rights, legal positivism and critiques of universality. Historical and philosophical texts frame debates about dignity, life and reproductive rights, punishment, religious freedom, expression and democracy. Close engagement with legal and philosophical arguments supports independent moral positions.
selectedCourseEvidence.discipline: Human rights law; Legal philosophy; Ethics
selectedCourseEvidence.topics: Human-rights generations and justifications; UDHR and its formation; UN and European human-rights protection; Natural law and natural rights; Legal positivism and cultural relativism; Universality and statelessness; Human dignity; Right to life and reproductive rights; Torture and punishment; Freedom of religion; Freedom of expression; Democracy
selectedCourseEvidence.methods: Treaty and legal-text analysis; Judicial and treaty-body case-law research; Case-law analysis; Philosophical text and argument analysis

selectedCourseEvidence.description2: Introduces rules, institutions and politics of public international law. Covers treaties, the UN, armed conflict, war crimes, refugee protection and climate change. Students analyse cases, debate issues and produce a podcast connecting law to global challenges.
selectedCourseEvidence.name: Introduction to Public International Law
selectedCourseEvidence.profile: Introduces public international law through its sources, theories, institutions and relationship to domestic legal systems. Legal principles are applied to responsibility, force, armed conflict, international crime, human rights, economic relations and environmental protection. The later course examines self-determination, Third World approaches, soft law, compliance and treaty politics. Case exercises develop legal reasoning, while a research podcast critically investigates a political dimension of international law.

selectedCourseEvidence.methods: Identification and interpretation of international legal instruments; Judgment and case-law analysis; Application of legal principles to factual scenarios; Legal, empirical and normative critique; Research podcast development

selectedCourseEvidence.description2: Explores constitutional law and state organisation, using a comparative approach. Covers constitutionalism, separation of powers, judicial review, federalism and fundamental rights, and discusses constitution‑making, religious constitutions and constitutional backsliding.
selectedCourseEvidence.name: Comparative Constitutional Law
selectedCourseEvidence.profile: Compares constitutional structures, institutions and rights across legal systems and introduces administrative law. Students examine constitutional features, federalism, legislatures, executive relationships, courts, judicial review and human rights. The administrative component addresses public participation, remedies and procedural fairness. A staged booklet compares two constitutions, supported by legal interpretation, case-law analysis and application of principles to hypothetical facts.
selectedCourseEvidence.topics: Constitutional origins and fundamental features; Federalism and decentralization; Parliaments and lawmaking; Governments and heads of state; Court systems and judicial review; Constitutional rights; EU constitutional order; Administrative-law functions; Public participation; Administrative remedies; Procedural fairness, discretion and legitimate expectations

selectedCourseEvidence.description2: Introduces the EU legal order. Studies institutions, framework, citizenship and the internal market using problem‑based exercises and guest lectures.

candidateStopping.assessment: The closest public-governance route, the workplace change and digital-organisation route, and the climate-governance route arise from separate target-specific interest clusters and organise study around different questions. Each has a coherent 24-course curriculum, passes feasibility, and differs from each other by at least ten courses. Three is the maximum. Re-audit retains three only after actual-content/weight review: the organizational option removes literary stylistics and creative poetry/performance, adds ethical and emotion-theory foundations, and uses modern sociology before advanced civil-society study. The climate option is a distinct combined domain-science/public-governance pathway, not an assertion that chemistry or energy engineering replaces administration. No specific merger, HR credential, clinical, teacher or digital-society master outcome is guaranteed. Current repair replaces overlapping rhetoric in the organisational composition with comparative constitutional/administrative accountability; same concept retained. Pairwise differences remain11,10,16courses. Gender-inequality correspondence reconsidered from actual psychological safety/minority survey content, not the old DiversityManagement label.
